prize_parts.citation: for empirical analyses of how technology and import competition reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B029 and listed B022 as an alternative. I now prefer B022 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. The move rests on three arguments and not on support counts. First, the objections I raised against my own B029 case have not been resolved in the exchange. Bresnahan's claim against Levinsohn or Berry is still open, and Fredriksson, who shares my preference, says he has softened his confidence on it. The methods-versus-discovery question is also unanswered, and the members with the closest field expertise have not said the trio is settled. I cannot resolve these from the evidence supplied. Second, B022 has a defensible attribution core once the citation is narrowed. The China-shock papers are joint work by Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and Autor is the common thread to the technology and tasks strand. Tying the citation to the empirical evidence on labour demand and local adjustment avoids claiming task-model theory whose originators sit outside the credited set. Third, the work asks a first-order question about who bears the cost of technological and trade change. It does so with transparent designs that have been replicated, re-analysed and contested for about a decade. Contested magnitudes are part of that record. They do not undo the finding that adjustment is slow and costly. As a macroeconomist working on technology and inequality, I also think the evidence on where and for whom labour demand shifts is the empirical counterpart to the aggregate models my own field builds, so I am wary of over-weighting it for that reason and say so in the conflict note. B029 stays an alternative because I still judge the BLP framework a prize-level discovery with a mature record and clean core attribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the size and persistence of the China-shock effects are still contested, and shift-share identification has been criticised. A prize here could be read as rewarding a research design and measurement programme more than a conceptual advance. The task framework has originators outside the credited set (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane), and the 2024 prize on technology and institutions is thematically close. The Committee would need a citation that does not overreach. Katz has a real claim to the earlier skill-premium literature, and the three-name cap forces his exclusion from this part. I also have not shown that B022 beats B012 on common criteria. B012 has a very clean two-name attribution and a long record of confirmation on firm-level data. My preference for B022 is a judgement about the breadth of the question and the people-and-places evidence, and it could reasonably go the other way. Finally, my own earlier case for B029 shows how much of my ranking depends on how I weigh attribution against maturity, so I do not treat the change as a scientific verdict on B029.

responses.point: Hassler proposes only Autor and Hanson for B022 and sees credit as blurred between task-based theory and the empirical China-shock work. He also notes thematic proximity to the 2024 prize. In his round-1 reply to me, he kept B029 below B012 because of the Bresnahan dispute and the methods-prize reading.
responses.response: I take the blur seriously, and it is why my citation names the empirical evidence on technology and import competition and not task-model theory. I disagree on Dorn. The China-shock papers are joint work by Autor, Dorn and Hanson, so dropping him from a citation built on them creates an attribution gap in the best-documented strand. A two-name prize would be defensible if the Committee anchored on the task-and-trade synthesis, and I would not oppose it. On the 2024 prize, I see overlap in theme but not in the core result. That is a timing judgement and not a merit judgement. I accept your point on B029. The Bresnahan question and the methods reading are the reasons I have moved off it.

responses.point: Fredriksson keeps B029 first. He argues that the BLP trio is the cleanest cut, that the citation should name market power, substitution and welfare and not the estimator, and that he is less sure about Bresnahan than his opening suggested.
responses.response: I agree that the citation can be framed around market power and welfare, and I still think the BLP framework is prize-level. But I could not answer the question we both left open, which is whether Bresnahan's early demand-estimation work should displace Berry or Levinsohn. Only four members ranked B029 in the opening. I do not treat that as a merit signal, but it means no member with strong field expertise has tested the attribution against us. I would be willing to return to B029 if that attribution argument were settled, and I keep it as my first alternative. For now, B022 has a cleaner credited set and a longer record of scrutiny.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B022 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She argues the China-shock trio is the cleanest basis for a three-person limit, and that the task framework's wider credit and the contested magnitudes are the main weaknesses. She also asked the B029 supporters how they separate the methods contribution from the findings it enabled.
responses.response: Her question to the B029 supporters is the one I could not settle, which contributes to my move. I think the methods enabled findings on market power and welfare, but the Committee could still reasonably read the prize as a methods prize soon after 2021. I agree with her view on B022 attribution and on the persistence debate. I would add that the debate concerns the size and duration of the effects, not whether the adjustment costs exist, so it argues for careful wording and for the Scientific Background to address re-analyses directly.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B022 first and moved from two names to three. He argues that the persistence debate concerns size and duration and not existence, and that B012 and B022 cover different ground. He says he could not weigh the methodological claims of empirical IO.
responses.response: I agree that the persistence debate argues for citation wording and not against the award. I also accept that B012 and B022 cover different ground, which means the comparison has to rest on common criteria: originality, breadth of confirmation and attributable credit. On those, I see B012 as stronger on attribution and clarity of mechanism, and B022 as stronger on the breadth of the question and on how long the evidence has been contested. I recognise that is a judgement and not a measurement. Your candour about not being able to weigh empirical IO is fair, and it is part of why I have not pressed B029 as a first choice.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B012 first with Melitz and Helpman. He argues for a tight two-person award, trade's absence from the prize since 2008, more than two decades of microdata confirmation, and breadth into macro and growth. He lists B022 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I said in round 1 that B012 is the strongest competitor on clarity of credit, and I still think so. I would not rank trade's absence since 2008 as scientific merit, but it is a legitimate timing consideration for the Committee. Where I differ is on weighting. B022 addresses who gains and loses and where, which a theory-of-trade prize does not. B012 has the cleaner two-name credit and the longer confirmation record on firm data. If the Committee decides the unresolved task-framework credit and the shift-share critiques outweigh B022's breadth, I would support B012 over B029, and that is why it is my second alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee can word the B022 citation so that it rests on the China-shock and local-labour-market evidence without claiming task-model theory whose originators (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane) are outside the credited set.
How far shift-share identification critiques and re-analyses of persistence should qualify the award, and whether the Scientific Background can address them directly.
Whether B022 should rank above B012 on common criteria. I see this as a close judgement about breadth of question versus cleanness of credit.
Whether Bresnahan's claim should displace Berry or Levinsohn on B029, and whether the Committee would read that ballot as a methods prize after 2021. This stays unresolved for me.
How much weight the thematic proximity of the 2024 prize deserves, and whether it is a timing judgement or a merit judgement.
My recollection of contribution details and credit shares is general knowledge and has not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Autor, Hanson or Dorn appears in my supplied profile, and my long-term co-authors (Hassler, Smith, Ríos-Rull, Violante, Greenwood, Hercowitz, Tsyvinski, Olovsson, Boppart) are not credited names on B022. My research on capital-skill complementarity and technology and inequality is adjacent to the skill-premium literature around B022. I treat that as subject expertise and not as evidence of merit, and I do not propose Katz. I have co-authored with Timo Boppart (co-opted member, B012 supporter) and John Hassler (chair, B012 supporter), neither of whom is a credited name on my preferred or alternative ballots. For my alternative B029, none of Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn appears in my profile. I no longer propose B047, but I note that institutional proximity to Torsten Persson in Stockholm might exist that my profile does not record. These are disclosed and not adjudicated.
